newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Forex dealers speculate on who lost on the baht.
newsitem.headline: Forex dealers speculate on who lost on the baht.

text.p: Speculative attacks on the Thai baht have been halted, at least for the time being, and the latest round of speculation among dealers is, who were the big losers?

Harry's Bar on Singapore's trendy Boat Quay has long been a haunt of largely expatriate financial market brokers and traders. On Friday the topic of conversation amongst them was devoted largely to the after-effects of the failed baht attack.
"There really has been blood on the streets and some banks are still bleeding. This has cost some people their jobs," the head of trading at a European bank here said.
Starting on Wednesday, May 14 the Bank of Thailand was forced to spend billions of dollars defending the baht as wave after wave of speculative selling hit the currency.

The speculators had decided a combination of a high current account deficit, economic and financial market woes and rumours of instability in the Thai cabinet were good reason to launch an attack on currency.

On Wednesday the Thai central bank fixed the baht mid-rate at 25.86 baht to the dollar. But the selling pushed the currency down to around 26.70 at one point, way outside the supposed two satang trading range.

The central bank, along with other central banks, stepped in to buy baht and also reacted by making it extremely expensive for speculators to short the baht, that is sell baht they did not own hoping to cover the position at a lower rate later.

By squeezing short-term interest rates for foreigners higher -- at one stage the tomorrow/next rate for two day funds hit a staggering annualised equivalent of 2,000 percent -- the central bank saw the speculators off and the baht recovered.

One foreign exchange broker in Harry's Bar said that a trader at a French firm had managed to lose US$22 million on a tomorrow/next position in just a day. "They sacked him straight away," the broker added.
At least two U.S. investment banks were said to have racked up losses of anything up to US$120 million each while European banks were also rumoured to have lost heavily.
The head of trading at a European bank gave one example of how easy it had been to lose, or make, money.

"If you took a $10 (million) long position in six month baht forwards on Tuesday, you'd have been down around US$80,000 by Wednesday. I suppose that's manageable and you could decide to run (keep) it," he said.
"But on Thursday the rates moved so suddenly, so violently, you're losing a fortune. On the Friday morning you'd have been down $440,000."
He also noted that a $10 million position was pretty small. "Call it a $50 million position and its a $2.2 million loss in three days. Grim," he said.
So who won?

The view among the Harry's Bar crowd was summed up by the foreign exchange broker. "Who won? The Bank of Thailand for one. They saw the speculators off and were long of baht. And the Thai banks. They're getting cheap domestic funds and lending at a huge profit offshore."
A trader contacted by Reuters at a Thai bank in Bangkok concurred.

"Most Thai banks did not make much money from forex gains but we did gain a lot of interest rate profits after the central bank asked us to raise the cost of short-term baht swaps quoted for foreign buyers," he said.
Not since the day's of the Barings debacle in 1995 -- in which Harry's Bar regular Nick Leeson played a leading role -- has Boat Quay heard so much gossip about winners and losers.
-- Singapore newsroom (65) 870-3080
